meta.title: Local Full Fibre Networks Evaluation: work package one report — Synthesis of evidence and conclusions
meta.organisation: Building Digital UK; Department for Digital, Culture, Media & Sport
meta.topic: Full-fibre broadband deployment, supplier entry and local broadband market competition
meta.licence: Open Government Licence v3.0, except where otherwise stated

brief.intended_change: Improve the availability, affordability and choice of gigabit-capable broadband, while supporting a more competitive and sustainable broadband market.
brief.population: Broadband users, public-sector organisations and broadband suppliers in participating local areas.
brief.place: United Kingdom; the supplied synthesis covers case studies including Blackpool, Mid Sussex, Highlands, Portsmouth, Suffolk, Wolverhampton, Northern Ireland and Tay Cities.
brief.time_horizon: Retrospective assessment of market changes following LFFN projects; the supplied text does not specify a common follow-up period.
brief.intervention: The Local Full Fibre Networks programme provided public funding for local full-fibre connectivity projects, including connections to public-sector sites and infrastructure used by broadband suppliers. Project funding amounts, duration and connection targets are not specified in the supplied synthesis.
brief.context: Suppliers were undertaking substantial commercially funded expansion alongside other public broadband programmes. Their existing geographical commitments, private capital and national rollout strategies differed substantially.
brief.outcome_first: Develop a theory of change for improving the availability, affordability and choice of gigabit-capable broadband in local areas across the United Kingdom. Include the intended contribution to a more competitive and sustainable broadband market.
brief.intervention_first: Develop a theory of change for the Local Full Fibre Networks programme in participating UK local areas. The programme funds local full-fibre connectivity projects and aims to improve broadband availability, affordability and choice while supporting a more competitive and sustainable market.

context: Private investment was the primary driver of supplier entry; all examined alt-nets had secured substantial private capital before LFFN.
F&W Networks and Fibrus had pre-existing geographical strategies focused on Sussex and Northern Ireland respectively; national operators CityFibre and ITS had more competing rollout options.
Private investment and larger public programmes, including Project Stratum, were principal drivers of network expansion outside LFFN.
VMO2's gigabit upgrades and migration to full fibre formed part of national programmes independent of LFFN.
Delivery model, supplier type and local market conditions substantially affected the strength of observed outcomes.
Limited visibility of CNI infrastructure and suppliers' preference for owning their networks restricted infrastructure sharing.
Consolidation pressures affected the alt-net sector, particularly the outlook for F&W Networks.

key_claims.claim: LFFN can bring forward supplier entry by removing local cost and risk barriers, particularly for suppliers not already committed to the area.

verdict.raw: LFFN did contribute to supplier entry in some locations, but this effect was highly variable across suppliers and areas and was strongest where LFFN aligned with commercial interest but removed key barriers to entry. ... LFFN funding directly enabled the company to enter multiple local markets (Highlands, Portsmouth, Suffolk and Wolverhampton) ... ITS reported that its entry into Blackpool was a direct consequence of CNI infrastructure being available ... In Northern Ireland, LFFN did not influence entry: Fibrus was already active in the market
verdict.quote: strongest where LFFN aligned with commercial interest but removed key barriers to entry

key_claims.claim: Public-sector fibre connections and shared infrastructure can accelerate rollout and enable incremental network extensions, without necessarily changing suppliers' underlying investment plans.

verdict.raw: LFFN generally made an enabling contribution, helping to accelerate or slightly extend rollout, rather than fundamentally changing investment plans or delivering large-scale coverage uplift. ... there is no evidence that LFFN contributed to expanded coverage or accelerated deployment for VMO2. ... both Fibrus and Openreach NI indicated that FFNI allowed them to serve additional premises ... The scale of these additional connections is uncertain ... Openreach in Tay Cities reported that LFFN accelerated deployment in some locations, particularly in Perth ... In Mid Sussex, F&W Networks had already decided to enter the market for commercial reasons; CNI infrastructure simply made delivery faster and easier
verdict.quote: an enabling contribution, helping to accelerate or slightly extend rollout

key_claims.claim: Additional customers and public contracts can support alt-net growth, but LFFN's larger contribution may be delivery capability and credibility rather than direct short-term revenue.
key_claims.where: Section 1.3, Claim 3; section 3.2; revised diagram, section 3.3

verdict.raw: In most cases, the direct impact of LFFN on revenues is likely to have been modest ... ITS and CityFibre, reported that LFFN areas accounted for a noticeable share of their revenues at certain points in time ... This makes it difficult to establish a clear counterfactual or to isolate LFFN’s direct revenue effect. ... For other alt-nets, such as F&W Networks and Fibrus, the contribution of LFFN to revenue growth appears to be limited to those incremental premises ... participation in LFFN provided an early opportunity to deliver large-scale public-sector contracts, helping them to build a demonstrable track record ... This effect was cited by both CityFibre ... and Fibrus
verdict.quote: its more important effect appears to have been in building credibility and strengthening the foundations for future expansion

key_claims.claim: A visible government commitment to full fibre would change operators' strategic rollout plans and stimulate additional private network investment.

verdict.raw: There is no evidence that LFFN acted as a wider market signal that influenced operators’ strategic investment decisions. Interviewees consistently reported that their organisations already had established strategies and long-term rollout plans for fibre deployment, and that these were not altered in response to the programme.
verdict.quote: these were not altered in response to the programme

key_claims.claim: Successful public-sector contracts can strengthen an alt-net's credibility and help it attract private finance, depending on its development stage and existing backing.

verdict.raw: For the CNI alt-nets (F&W Networks and ITS) there is no evidence that access to LFFN-funded CNI infrastructure helped them attract private investment. ... investors may initially view the CNI model as less favourable, preferring operators that own their underlying infrastructure. ... Anchor-tenancy agreements, including those associated with early LFFN Wave 1 projects, helped provide lenders with confidence and unlock working capital. ... LFFN contracts in later years were unlikely to have played a material role in securing further investment ... LFFN made a substantial contribution to Fibrus’s ability to attract investment.
verdict.quote: LFFN played an important role for Fibrus, had limited or no effect for most CNI suppliers

key_claims.claim: LFFN-supported supplier entry can prompt incumbents to accelerate rollout or improve their networks, but this response is not general across local markets.
key_claims.where: Section 1.6, Claim 6; section 3.2; revised diagram, section 3.3

verdict.raw: There is only limited evidence from case studies that LFFN provoked a competitive response from incumbents, with effects varying substantially by area. The clearest indication of a competitive response comes from Wolverhampton ... Point Topic data ... shows a marked increase in Openreach’s coverage coinciding with CityFibre’s deployment. ... the rollout data generally shows either very limited expansion by Openreach, or that Openreach’s footprint was already growing before CityFibre entered the market ... In most areas, the VMO2 footprint has remained largely unchanged ... national upgrade programmes, with no indication that they were triggered by LFFN-funded competition.
verdict.quote: only limited evidence ... with effects varying substantially by area

key_claims.claim: Entry and expansion of wholesale fibre networks allow more ISPs to offer gigabit packages, increasing consumer choice where LFFN adds coverage.

verdict.raw: There is consistent evidence that LFFN increased ISP choice in areas where it facilitated CityFibre’s entry into the market. ... in all five LFFN areas where it entered (Blackpool, Highlands, Portsmouth, Suffolk and Wolverhampton) its presence led to the availability of packages from Zen Fibre and Vodafone. ... In Northern Ireland ... LFFN’s contribution to increasing ISP choice is limited to the incremental footprints created through FFNI ... A similar pattern is observed in Tay Cities
verdict.quote: consistent evidence ... in areas where it facilitated CityFibre’s entry

key_claims.claim: Alternative networks and lower delivery costs can increase price competition and access to cheaper gigabit broadband packages.
key_claims.where: Section 1.8, Claim 8; section 1.7 on future competition; section 3.1

verdict.raw: There is strong evidence from the CNI and CityFibre case studies that LFFN has helped make broadband more affordable ... In Blackpool, ISPs using CityFibre consistently offered the lowest-cost packages at a range of speed thresholds ... In Mid Sussex, Hey Broadband ... offered the cheapest deals on the market for most speed ranges ... CNI enabled them to deliver higher-capacity services at lower cost ... Similar patterns were observed in the CityFibre case study areas ... In Northern Ireland, Fibrus also offers the cheapest deals ... for the subset of premises that gained access specifically through FFNI, LFFN has directly increased the availability of affordable full-fibre options.
verdict.quote: strong evidence ... that LFFN has helped make broadband more affordable

key_claims.claim: Demonstrating anchor-tenancy and shared-infrastructure delivery models can increase councils' confidence in using them and lower barriers to supplier entry.

verdict.raw: LFFN supported the use and wider awareness of two delivery models ... both of which pre-dated the programme ... LFFN helped to formalise its use across multiple areas and provided other councils with greater confidence to adopt the model. ... the programme played an important role in raising its profile and encouraging uptake by local authorities in Blackpool and Mid Sussex. ... both the anchor tenancy and CNI approaches have demonstrated clear strengths in supporting supplier entry and improving consumer outcomes
verdict.quote: provided other councils with greater confidence to adopt the model

key_claims.claim: Shared passive infrastructure can produce a more coordinated and efficient market only if suppliers know about it and choose to share assets.

verdict.raw: the broader market-shaping ambitions of CNI, such as enabling a more coordinated and efficient approach to network deployment, have been realised only to a limited degree. This reflects a combination of factors, including limited visibility of CNI infrastructure among some market participants and a continued preference among many alt-nets to deploy their own networks, rather than widespread take-up of shared assets.
verdict.quote: have been realised only to a limited degree

key_claims.claim: Supplier entry and wholesale access improvements can sustain greater choice and affordability when supported suppliers remain financially resilient.
key_claims.where: Section 2.2, Sustainability of alt-nets and market changes

verdict.raw: most of the alt-nets supported through LFFN are in a relatively strong long-term position ... ITS reported substantial recent growth supported by strategic acquisitions, substantial funding rounds ... CityFibre ... maintains its ambition to reach 8 million premises ... Fibrus has raised several rounds of investment ... The picture is more uncertain for F&W Networks ... a strategic partnership with Fusion Fibre Group ... may provide additional operational and financial resilience. ... In areas where LFFN stimulated supplier entry or expanded wholesale access ... the resulting increases in choice and affordability are also likely to persist
verdict.quote: the resulting increases in choice and affordability are also likely to persist

overall.raw: The evidence from the case studies provides a mixed picture of LFFN’s influence on broadband markets. Several elements of the theory of change are supported, while others show limited or no evidence.
overall.quote: a mixed picture of LFFN’s influence on broadband markets

conclusions.summary: LFFN enabled supplier entry in specific areas, modest extensions or acceleration of existing networks, and improved affordability and choice where competitive wholesale networks entered. It strengthened the credibility of some alt-nets, notably Fibrus, but direct revenue effects were generally modest. Wider market-signalling effects were not observed. Competitive responses from incumbents were limited, with the clearest evidence in Wolverhampton. CNI lowered some barriers to entry but did not produce widespread infrastructure sharing. Most supported alt-nets appeared relatively well positioned for continued operation, although F&W Networks' position was more uncertain. Grey outcomes represent partial or uneven evidence rather than necessarily no impact; only the wider market-signalling pathway was consistently ruled out across all case studies.
recommendations: Read the diagram alongside the narrative findings, which explain how and where LFFN contributed to outcomes in practice.
Interpret the diagram with care: the strength of evidence depends on delivery model, supplier type and local market conditions, and grey shading does not generally mean no impact.

open_questions: The figures are HTML images without page numbers; figure_pages is empty and verdict pages are null.
The revised diagram in section 3.3 is transcribed once. The initial ToC is the earlier version of the same theory, not a separate diagram.
The single Outcomes heading does not distinguish short- from long-term outcomes. All boxes under it are mapped to outcome_short without imposing a new temporal subdivision.

Input wiring shares junctions: the BDUK line joins routes to deployment and facilitating competitive procurement. Links l2 and l3 record those branches with medium confidence; the shared routing does not provide separate arrowheads for every input-to-activity relationship.

Grey shading combines limited, mixed and absent evidence. For b26 and b28, the supplied narrative does not give a separate, precise node-level classification; partly records the combined grey category and should not be read as evidence of a measured partial effect.

Unshaded boxes are not automatically treated as achieved. The supplied synthesis does not separately assess broadband reliability, satisfaction, wellbeing, productivity, underserved-area capability or achievement of 99% coverage by 2032.
The synthesis names case studies and Point Topic data but supplies no author-year or DOI references; studies arrays are therefore empty.
No definitions of evidence_level A/B/C were supplied. B is used provisionally for this case-study-based ex-post synthesis.
The supplied synthesis does not specify programme funding amounts, dosage, project dates or a common evaluation follow-up period.

The figure contains no internal arrows connecting individual results inside its framed groups. Links to those groups remain at container level; narrative claims about individual results are retained in key_claims and box verdicts.
